lesson.title: Measuring the Right Thing: What Makes a Test Valid
lesson.summary: Validity asks whether a test actually measures what it claims to measure, and includes content, criterion, and construct validity as distinct standards of evidence.
lesson.body:
Validity asks a deceptively simple question about a test: does it actually measure what it claims to measure? A standardized test, discussed in the previous chapter, can be administered with perfect consistency and still fail this basic requirement if the content or the score simply does not reflect the underlying trait or ability it is supposed to capture. A driving test that only asked written questions about car engine mechanics, for instance, might be perfectly standardized, but it would have poor validity as a measure of someone's actual ability to drive safely.

Psychologists generally distinguish among several related forms of validity. Content validity concerns whether a test's items adequately cover the full range of the material or skill it is meant to assess, which matters a great deal for something like a classroom final exam that should represent everything taught during the course, not just a narrow slice of it. Criterion validity concerns whether test scores correlate with some independent, real world outcome. This is sometimes split further into concurrent validity, where the test and the outcome are measured at roughly the same time, such as a new depression screening questionnaire compared against an existing clinical diagnosis, and predictive validity, where the test is used to forecast a future outcome, such as an admissions test being used to predict later academic performance.

Construct validity is the broadest and, in many ways, the most theoretically demanding form: it asks whether a test truly captures the underlying psychological construct, such as intelligence, anxiety, or extraversion, that it claims to measure, rather than something else that merely happens to correlate with it. Establishing construct validity typically requires accumulating evidence from many different studies and comparisons over time, rather than a single simple check.

It helps to distinguish these more rigorous forms of validity from face validity, which is simply whether a test looks, on the surface, like it measures what it claims to measure. A test can have strong face validity and weak actual validity, or the reverse. This matters because test developers sometimes have to balance a test looking appropriate to test takers against a test performing well by more rigorous statistical standards.

Validity and standardization address different concerns, and a test needs both to be genuinely useful. Standardization makes sure the test is given fairly and consistently. Validity makes sure the resulting scores actually mean something about the trait the test was built to assess. As the next chapter will show, there is also a third essential property, reliability, and the relationship between reliability and validity turns out to be one of the more important and counterintuitive ideas in psychological measurement.
